items.headline: Cellectis scraps CAR-T pipeline in gene editing pivot
items.preview: Cellectis is abandoning its CAR-T programs to focus on gene editing for cardiovascular disease.
items.article:
French biotech Cellectis is abandoning development of its two internal allogeneic CAR-T programs and repositioning itself as an in vivo gene editing company focused initially on cardiovascular disease.

Why this matters: The move is a dramatic reset for one of Europe’s pioneers of off-the-shelf CAR-T. Cellectis is stopping development of lasme-cel in relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia and eti-cel in non-Hodgkin lymphoma, while looking for partners for both assets.

The new strategy centers on two preclinical cardiovascular programs: HEAL-101 and HEAL-201, both designed to alter gene activity without creating double-strand DNA breaks. Cellectis plans to realign its workforce and operations while maintaining cell therapy partnerships. Investors reacted negatively, with shares falling 43% following the announcement.

items.headline: BioNTech adds clinical weight to its oncology pivot at WCLC 2026
items.preview: BioNTech presents promising oncology data at WCLC, highlighting its shift from mRNA to antibodies.
items.article:
New data from the World Conference on Lung Cancer in Seoul are giving BioNTech’s oncology strategy more substance beyond its mRNA platform. Gotistobart has shown a marked survival benefit in previously treated squamous NSCLC, while the company’s leading bispecific antibody pumitamig continues to generate encouraging signals across tumor types.

Why this matters: BioNTech is building an oncology portfolio around antibodies, bispecifics, and combination approaches. The most advanced clinical readout comes from gotistobart, which achieved a median overall survival of 18.5 months in a Phase III study, significantly outperforming docetaxel.

The company is also presenting longer-term data for pumitamig in mesothelioma, indicating potential as a pan-tumor combination backbone. The results suggest that BioNTech’s oncology pipeline is acquiring the breadth and clinical maturity needed to transition from a focus on mRNA vaccines to a multi-platform oncology company.

items.headline: Cellectis quits CAR-T and pivots to ‘in vivo’ gene editing
items.preview: Cellectis shifts focus from CAR-T therapies to gene editing for cardiovascular diseases.
items.article:
Cellectis is giving up on donor-derived cell therapies and shifting its focus to gene editing medicines, stating that the commercial and clinical landscape for CAR-T treatments has changed materially. This decision dramatically extends Cellectis’ road to a marketed medicine, as it ends work on clinical-stage treatments and turns to therapies that haven’t been tested in humans.

Why this matters: Cellectis claimed that its new strategy represents the most effective use of its financial and operational resources. However, investors expressed disappointment, leading to a significant drop in share prices.

The new drugs will focus on cardiovascular disease treatments, including HEAL-101 and HEAL-201, both of which are still in preclinical development. Cellectis will also seek strategic partnerships to maximize the value of its existing CAR-T assets.

items.headline: Scholar Rock SMA drug approved by FDA
items.preview: The FDA approves Isembyld for spinal muscular atrophy, marking a significant treatment advance.
items.article:
The Food and Drug Administration has approved a new medication for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), called apitegromab, to be sold as Isembyld. The treatment is cleared for use alongside existing therapies in adults and children over 2 years old, with an annual list price of about $310,000.

Why this matters: Isembyld represents a significant advancement in SMA treatment, which previously had no approved medicines. The drug blocks myostatin, a protein that limits muscle growth, and has shown potential to improve motor function significantly.

Despite some manufacturing delays that previously held up approval, Scholar Rock is now positioned to launch Isembyld, which is seen as a therapeutic breakthrough for SMA patients.

items.headline: AZ’s camizestrant miss narrows oral SERD treatment settings
items.preview: AstraZeneca's camizestrant fails in Phase III trial, prompting a focus on ESR1 mutation patients.
items.article:
AstraZeneca's camizestrant, an oral selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD), did not meet the primary endpoint of progression-free survival in the Phase III Serena-4 trial for first-line HER2-negative, estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer.

Why this matters: This setback suggests that focusing on patients with ESR1 mutations may be necessary to prove efficacy for oral SERDs. The failure comes amidst several significant readouts for non-small cell lung cancer therapies reported at the World Conference on Lung Cancer.

The implications of this miss may lead to a reevaluation of treatment strategies for oral SERDs in breast cancer settings.
